items.title: A Google-like search engine for single-cell RNA data could answer previously impossible questions
items.excerpt: Max Delbruck Center researchers built Malva, a search platform that queries millions of single cells using raw sequence information alone, finding RNA isoforms and rare variants without reference genomes or huge downloads. The team frames it as infrastructure that both scientists and AI tools can query in seconds.
items.why: Single-cell AI: turns the field's biggest dataset problem into a search problem, and is explicitly built to be queried by AI agents.

items.title: Virtual cell model could accelerate protein-degrader therapy design
items.excerpt: Weill Cornell Medicine built a computational model of the cell that identifies which targets are worth pursuing for protein-degrader drugs and guides optimization, potentially cutting years off development timelines.
items.why: Computational biology / virtual cell: modeling replaces a chunk of wet-lab trial and error in a hot drug modality.

items.title: Going beyond simple models of neural networks: Extended mean-field theory offers a better approach
items.excerpt: Princeton physicists found that standard mean-field theory fails to reproduce real neuron activity, but an extended version that carries full probability distributions matched recordings from over 1,000 mouse brain neurons.
items.why: Physics of neural networks meets neuroscience: a theory upgrade that changes how both brains and artificial nets are modeled.

items.title: An AI tool for prioritizing candidate biomarkers from wearable sensor data
items.excerpt: Google Research describes a pipeline that mines continuous wearable sensor streams to surface and rank candidate digital biomarkers, narrowing an enormous hypothesis space before clinical validation.
items.why: AI hypothesis generation applied to health data: the model does the candidate screening step that used to be a research program.

items.title: How mobility gives language models a deeper understanding of place
items.excerpt: Google Research shows that grounding language models in aggregated human mobility patterns gives them a far richer representation of places than text alone, improving geospatial reasoning tasks.
items.why: Foundation models for science: behavioral data as a new grounding signal for LLMs, relevant to geography and urban research.

items.title: FAU Researchers Use Quantum Machine Learning to Predict Heart Disease
items.excerpt: Florida Atlantic University researchers benchmarked quantum feature maps and quantum classifiers on clinical data from 918 patients, reporting 90.26% accuracy for heart disease prediction and mapping where quantum encoding helps versus classical baselines.
items.why: Quantum machine learning tested on a real clinical dataset rather than a toy benchmark - a rare concrete data point on QML's practical footing.

items.title: Does Computer Science Need Computers?
items.excerpt: A look at theoretical computer science as a mathematical discipline whose results about what is computable and how fast now set the ceiling for what AI systems can ever do.
items.why: Theory context for the empirical AI boom: which limits are engineering problems and which are proofs.

items.title: AI models flub these intelligence tests. Can you fare any better?
items.excerpt: A set of reasoning puzzles that current frontier models consistently fail, presented so readers can attempt them too - a hands-on look at where machine and human cognition diverge.
items.why: Cognitive-science framing of AI benchmarks: makes the failure modes legible instead of abstract.

items.title: New AI uses a fresh approach to reasoning that's potentially much cheaper
items.excerpt: Researchers describe a reasoning architecture that departs from standard chain-of-thought scaling and, they report, runs up to 11 times cheaper than a leading OpenAI model on comparable tasks.
items.why: Machine reasoning research: cost per inference is what decides whether AI can be run at scientific scale.

items.title: OpenAI funds research to try to stop AI from being used to make bioweapons
items.excerpt: As AI protein and virus design tools mature, researchers are building evaluation methods to detect when a model is helping someone design something dangerous - work that is running well ahead of any regulation.
items.why: The safety layer of AI protein design: new evaluation science for generative biology, not just policy talk.

items.title: How Frontier Medicines plans to drug the undruggable with AI and a chemical library
items.excerpt: Frontier Medicines pairs a covalent chemical library with machine learning to find binding pockets on proteins long considered undruggable, using computation to decide which chemistry to run next.
items.why: AI drug discovery as a lab method: model-guided selection of which covalent probes to synthesize and test.

items.title: Shared-memory AI system lets microscope components coordinate in real time
items.excerpt: Janelia and Anthropic researchers built the Model Hardware Standard, a shared-memory layer that lets heterogeneous microscope components talk to each other and to an AI that can watch and adjust an experiment while it runs. Setup time dropped from months to days.
items.why: Lab automation: an AI that steers instruments mid-experiment, which is the missing plumbing for self-driving labs.

items.title: Researchers develop AI framework to optimize solid oxide electrolysis cell operation
items.excerpt: A Seoul National University of Science and Technology team replaced 6,561 simulations with 17, using an AI-guided search that improved electrochemical performance 14% and cut temperature gradients by 80% in solid oxide electrolysis cells.
items.why: AI for energy materials: a concrete, quantified collapse of the simulation budget needed to design a device.

items.title: AI doesn't just play better chess - it manages complexity differently
items.excerpt: Complexity Science Hub and University of Parma researchers analyzed over 2,000 games and found engines sustain high board complexity far longer than humans, who simplify positions early even when their peak tension matches the machine's.
items.why: Quantifies a real cognitive difference between human and machine problem-solving using a measurable proxy for complexity tolerance.

items.title: How health systems are embracing chatbots to query and summarize patient records
items.excerpt: Hospitals are deploying LLM interfaces over electronic health records so clinicians can ask questions of a patient's chart in natural language rather than hunting through structured fields.
items.why: Clinical data practice shift: retrieval over messy real-world records is the same problem scientific literature search faces.
